title: Cosmology: Methodological Debates in the 1930s and 1940s

summaries.example: Imagine two teams trying to draw a map of a huge island. One team says, "First collect lots of measurements, then build the map." The other says, "Think of a clear map idea first, then check whether measurements fit it." The cosmologists in this debate faced a similar choice about how to build theories of the Universe.
summaries.summary: This entry tells the story of a major argument about how to study the Universe. New ideas from Einstein's general theory of relativity connected gravity with the shape of space and time. Later, Hubble's observations of a red shift in light from distant star systems encouraged many scientists to think that the Universe was expanding. Cosmologists then disagreed about method. Some favored starting with observations and building general rules from them. Others, especially E. A. Milne, favored proposing broad ideas first and then working out what those ideas predicted. Milne also questioned whether unseen shapes of space should be treated as real. The debate was energetic and sometimes harsh. Over time, parts of Milne's methods became respected, even though his own cosmological program later slowed. In 1948, Hermann Bondi and others developed steady-state cosmology, which said that the Universe always has the same large-scale appearance. The entry shows that philosophical questions about evidence, reasoning, and reality can help guide the development of science.
key_ideas: In the 1930s and 1940s, scientists argued about how cosmology should be done.
One group wanted theories to begin with observations and measurements.
Another group wanted scientists to imagine possible theories and then use reasoning to predict observations.
Einstein's general relativity changed ideas about gravity, space, and time.
Hubble's observations helped lead many scientists to accept an expanding universe.
Milne's ideas influenced later work, including Bondi's steady-state cosmology.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history shows that science is not only about collecting facts. Scientists must also decide how to form explanations, what can count as real, and how theories should be tested. Cosmology has few and difficult-to-obtain observations, so these questions became especially important. Studying the debate can help us understand why different scientists may interpret the same evidence in different ways.

important_terms.definition: The study of the Universe as a whole, including its structure, history, and possible changes.
A careful plan for how to investigate something and decide whether an explanation is good.
Information gained by looking, measuring, or doing experiments.
A suggested explanation that can be checked against what we observe.
The idea that gravity is connected with the shape of space and time, rather than being only a pulling force.
The idea that the Universe is getting larger, so many distant galaxies are moving farther apart.

questions_to_think_about: Should scientists always collect observations before making a theory?
Can a useful idea begin with imagination and mathematics?
Why might it be difficult to test ideas about the whole Universe?
What would count as good evidence that the Universe is changing?

summaries.example: Suppose two researchers study a newly discovered ecosystem that is difficult to visit. An inductive empiricist would emphasize gathering reliable measurements and generalizing from them. A hypothetico-deductivist might begin with a mathematically simple model, derive predictions, and then ask whether later measurements support or challenge it. Neither approach automatically succeeds; the comparison depends on the predictions, evidence, and assumptions involved.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how philosophical commitments shaped cosmology from the development of relativistic cosmology through the rise of steady-state theory. General relativity replaced the older picture of gravity as a force acting within fixed Euclidean space. It instead linked gravitation to the curvature of spacetime. Hubble's red-shift observations then encouraged the interpretation that the Universe was expanding, and LeMaître's expanding model became influential. Because cosmology had relatively scarce and difficult observations, scientists disagreed sharply about how theories should be constructed. The inductive-empiricist side treated observation as the foundation of knowledge and favored generalization from data. The opposing rationalist, hypothetico-deductive side allowed hypotheses to originate from broad principles and judged them by the observable consequences deduced from them. Milne joined this method to operationalism, which challenged the reality of theoretical structures not directly tied to observational operations. His kinematic relativity became a target of criticism but later influenced work by McCrea, Walker, Robertson, and Bondi. The entry presents the debate as historically important because it helped establish the methodological status of cosmology. Bondi's steady-state theory added a Popperian emphasis on falsifiability: a theory should make claims that observations could, in principle, disprove. Later observations of cosmic background radiation supplied evidence against the steady-state model, and Bondi accepted that consequence of his methodological position.
key_ideas: The central dispute concerned scientific methodology, though it also involved epistemology and metaphysics.
Inductive empiricists treated observations as the starting point for scientific knowledge and generalization.
Milne and other hypothetico-deductivists emphasized proposing hypotheses, deriving predictions, and testing those predictions.
Milne's operationalism rejected treating unobservable structures such as curved or expanding space as straightforward physical realities.
Relativistic cosmology and kinematic relativity were presented for a time as competing accounts that observations could not clearly distinguish.
Bondi combined Milne's deductive approach with Popper's demand that scientific theories be open to possible falsification.
summaries.why_it_matters: The episode illustrates that scientific theories depend on more than equations and observations alone. They also involve assumptions about what counts as evidence, whether unobservable structures are real, and how hypotheses should be judged. The debate is especially instructive because both sides claimed to defend scientific rigor, yet they disagreed about the proper relationship between reason and observation. It also shows how philosophical arguments can influence scientific research programs without replacing empirical testing.

important_terms.definition: The scientific study of the Universe as a whole, including its structure, development, and large-scale physical theories.
A view that scientific knowledge begins with sensory or experimental evidence, together with a method that generalizes from observed cases.
A view that theories may begin with proposed concepts or hypotheses, from which consequences are logically derived and compared with observations.
The position that theoretical entities referred to by successful scientific theories should be regarded as physically real.
A position associated in the entry with Milne: an entity counts as real only when its properties can be revealed through an observational procedure.
A general assumption that observers in different places should obtain the same broad picture of the Universe.
Einstein's theory in which gravity is represented through the curvature of spacetime, linking geometry with physical behavior.
A theory proposed in 1948 in which the Universe remains broadly unchanged over time, rather than developing from a definite origin.

questions_to_think_about: Does successful prediction support a theory even if its theoretical entities cannot be directly observed?
Can a cosmological principle function as a useful hypothesis rather than an observed generalization?
Why would limited evidence make philosophical assumptions more influential in cosmology?
Is a theory better if it is simpler, more mathematically unified, or more easily testable?
What kinds of observations could decide between rival cosmological theories?

summaries.example: Imagine trying to understand a sealed machine that you can inspect only once in a while. One investigator records every visible change and builds a rule from the records. Another invents several possible designs, predicts what each design would do, and checks the next inspection. The cosmologists' debate was similar, except their "machine" was the entire Universe and their observations were much harder to obtain.
summaries.summary: The entry explores a vigorous dispute among cosmologists and philosophers of science during the 1930s and 1940s. Its background was a revolution in thinking about the Universe. Einstein's general relativity changed gravity from a force acting inside fixed space into a phenomenon connected with curved spacetime. Hubble's observations of red-shifted light from distant star systems were widely interpreted as evidence that the Universe was expanding. This encouraged the growth of relativistic cosmology. Scientists then asked how this new science should work. The majority position combined explanatory realism with inductive empiricism: accepted theoretical entities could be real, and scientific knowledge was built by generalizing from observations. E. A. Milne challenged this combination. His operationalism allowed reality only for what could be connected to an observational operation, and his hypothetico-deductivism began with possible models and derived predictions from them. His cosmological principle was an example of a broad starting idea rather than a conclusion drawn directly from data. Critics such as Eddington and Dingle defended stronger forms of realism or induction, while other researchers recognized useful features in Milne's approach. By the late 1930s, his methods had gained respect even though observational evidence did not yet clearly choose between rival models. Bondi later joined Milne's deductive approach with Popper's requirement that scientific theories be vulnerable to falsification, using it to develop steady-state cosmology.
key_ideas: Cosmology became a new field after general relativity and observations of red-shifted light changed ideas about the Universe.
The main disagreement was whether observation or theoretical reasoning should lead the construction of a theory.
Milne used operationalism to challenge claims about curved space, expanding space, and spacetime.
His alternative, kinematic relativity, used measurements made through signals and clocks and was linked to a deductive method.
Some scientists criticized Milne's philosophy while finding parts of his physics interesting; others later adopted parts of his methods.
Bondi's steady-state cosmology extended this deductive tradition while requiring a theory to be testable and possibly disprovable.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps explain why scientific disagreement is not always simply a contest between facts and mistakes. Researchers may share observations but differ about what those observations can establish, how theories should begin, and what kinds of entities science may describe. Cosmology made these issues unusually visible because observations of the entire Universe are limited. The history also shows that a philosophical method can influence which scientific models are developed and how they are tested.

important_terms.definition: The study of the Universe on the largest scale: its shape, contents, history, and possible behavior.
A debate about the proper way to build, compare, and test scientific theories.
The view that science should begin with observations and use them to form broader generalizations.
The view that scientists can propose hypotheses and then logically derive predictions to compare with observations.
The idea that entities described by a successful theory may be real, even when they are not directly seen.
The idea that something should count as real only if an observation or procedure can reveal its properties.
The proposal that observers throughout the Universe should see the same general kind of cosmos.
A theory that connects gravity with the curvature of space and time.

questions_to_think_about: Can scientists reasonably propose a theory before they have much evidence?
Are unobservable parts of a theory meaningful if they help explain observations?
Why might the same cosmological principle be treated as either an observation-based rule or a starting assumption?
How does a theory become scientific if it must be open to disproof?
Why would a new science be especially likely to produce arguments about method?
